docs.text:
The following quantities are available at global level, which can be recorded using global recorders.

variable label physical meaning KE kinetic energy SE strain energy VE viscous energy NVE nonviscous viscous energy K stiffness matrix M mass matrix AMP amplitude

docs.title: Special Quantities
docs.text:
The following are some special quantities that are only available for certain models.

variable label physical meaning ED damper strain in Maxwell/Kelvin model VD damper strain rate in Maxwell/Kelvin model SD damper stress in Maxwell/Kelvin model ES spring strain in Maxwell/Kelvin model VS spring strain rate in Maxwell/Kelvin model SS spring stress defined in Maxwell/Kelvin model DAMAGE damage variable in phase field models DT tension damage DC compressive damage PP pore pressure VF volume fraction in Gurson related models LITR location iteration in Maxwell model BEAME beam end deformation BEAMS beam end resultant forces

docs.title: Recorder
docs.text:
Record Model Response

The available output types are listed in the OutputType file.

To control the folders to which the recorder will write the output, please check the OutputFolder file.

Not all quantities at every time step need to be stored. Only those explicitly specified will be stored as history output.

Currently, there are several types of recorders. Analysts can choose to record either element response at integration points (strain, stress, etc., some elements support response at elemental nodes) or nodal response at model nodes (displacement, velocity, acceleration, reaction, etc.). The third type supports the output of the summation of the same quantity of several nodes/elements. Alternatively, the analyst can record global quantities such as global stiffness/mass, global kinetic energy, etc.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Two types of format are supported. The output file can be either plain text or HDF5 file if the program is compiled with HDF5 support. The general form to define a record is as follows.

Recorder
recorder (1) plain (2) (3) [every 4] [5...]
recorder (1) hdf5 (2) (3) [every 4] [5...]
# (1) int, unique recorder tag
# (2) string, recorder type
# (3) string, output type
# [4] int, optional argument with leading keyword "every" to indicate the interval of recording,
# for example: "every 10" means the recorder will record the response every ten converged substeps.
# [5...] int, tags of elements/nodes, etc.

Alternatively, it is possible to use the following two equivalences.

Text Only
plainrecorder (1) (2) (3) [every 4] [5...]
hdf5recorder (1) (2) (3) [every 4] [5...]

There are some recorder types that do not need tags of elements/nodes as they record the response of the whole model.

docs.title: Eigen Recorder
docs.text:
Text Only
# to record eigenvalues and eigenvectors if current step is an eigenanalysis step
recorder (1) plain Eigen
recorder (1) hdf5 Eigen
# (1) int, unique recorder tag

docs.title: Modal Recorder
docs.text:
The Modal recorder extracts frequencies, mass-normalised mode shapes, participation factors and effective modal masses from an eigenanalysis step.

Text Only
recorder (1) hdf5 Modal (2...)
# (1) int, unique recorder tag
# (2...) string, DoF identifiers that define the influence directions

The recorder writes an HDF5 file. Please check ModalRecorder for the computed quantities and the data layout.

docs.title: Modal Force Recorder
docs.text:
The ModalForce recorder extracts the modal elastic forces from an eigenanalysis step. It writes the assembled nodal force vector and the element force vectors.

Text Only
recorder (1) hdf5 ModalForce
# (1) int, unique recorder tag

The recorder writes an HDF5 file. Please check ModalForceRecorder for the computed quantities and the data layout.

docs.title: Frame Recorder
docs.text:
Text Only
# to record response of the whole model, this one only supports HDF5
recorder (1) hdf5 Frame (3) [every 4]
# (1) int, unique recorder tag
# (3) string, output type
# [4] int, optional argument with leading keyword "every" to indicate the interval of recording,
# for example: "every 10" means the recorder will record the response every ten converged substeps.

docs.title: Visualization Recorder
docs.text:
Text Only
# to record response of the whole model and write to VTK files for visualisation, this one is enabled only with VTK support.
recorder (1) plain Visualisation (3) [every 4]
recorder (1) hdf5 Visualisation (3) [every 4]
# (1) int, unique recorder tag
# (3) string, output type
# [4] int, optional argument with leading keyword "every" to indicate the interval of recording,
# for example: "every 10" means the recorder will record the response every ten converged substeps.

The Visualisation will immediately write to the disk with incremental file names.

docs.title: Node Recorder
docs.text:
To record nodal response,

Text Only
recorder (1) plain Node (3) [every 4] [5...]
recorder (1) hdf5 GroupNode (3) [every 4] [5...]
# (1) int, unique recorder tag
# (3) string, output type
# [4] int, optional argument with leading keyword "every" to indicate the interval of recording,
# for example: "every 10" means the recorder will record the response every ten converged substeps.
# [5...] int, tags of nodes or node groups, etc.

If GroupNode is used, then the tags of node groups shall be used.

Nodal scalar response can be directly summed up by using the Sum recorder.

Text Only
recorder (1) plain Sum (3) [every 4] [5...]
recorder (1) hdf5 GroupSum (3) [every 4] [5...]
# (1) int, unique recorder tag
# (3) string, output type
# [4] int, optional argument with leading keyword "every" to indicate the interval of recording
# [5...] int, tags of nodes or node groups, etc.

It is handy to record the summation of nodal response, for example, the summation of nodal reaction force.

docs.title: Element Recorder
docs.text:
To record element response,

Text Only
recorder (1) plain Element (3) [every 4] [5...]
recorder (1) hdf5 GroupElement (3) [every 4] [5...]
# (1) int, unique recorder tag
# (3) string, output type
# [4] int, optional argument with leading keyword "every" to indicate the interval of recording,
# for example: "every 10" means the recorder will record the response every ten converged substeps.
# [5...] int, tags of elements or element groups, etc.

If GroupElement is used, then the tags of element groups shall be used.

docs.title: Global Recorder
docs.text:
Sometimes, it is necessary to record global quantities.

Currently, it is possible to record energy quantities.

Text Only
recorder (1) plain Global (3) [every 4]
recorder (1) hdf5 Global (3) [every 4]
# (1) int, unique recorder tag
# (3) string, output type
# [4] int, optional argument with leading keyword "every" to indicate the interval of recording,
# for example: "every 10" means the recorder will record the response every ten converged substeps.

The (3) can be:

  1. KE: kinetic energy
  2. SE: strain energy (potential energy)
  3. VE: energy dissipated via viscosity
  4. NVE: energy dissipated via non-viscosity
  5. MM: momentum
  6. K: global stiffness matrix, vectorised
  7. M: global mass matrix, vectorised

For energy terms, the recorder records two quantities computed from different sources: the first column is the summation of all corresponding energy terms collected from all valid elements; the second column is the global energy term.

The reason to have two different columns is to mainly account for the fact that some models/theories may impose global level energy dissipation.

A very direct example is the global damping models used in seismic engineering. Take the Rayleigh model as an example. Since it can be implemented in two ways, either apply linear combination of stiffness and mass at element level after computing elemental stiffness and mass (see Rayleigh Modifier), or globally after assembling global stiffness and mass (see RayleighNewmark). If the former is selected, each element can record its own energy dissipation term. If the latter is selected, the dissipated energy can only be computed from global stored quantities.

Some other models cannot be applied at element level, resulting in missing energy if those energy terms are only collected from elements.

As a rule of thumb, often two columns are equal to each other, if there is no global energy 'modifier'. Otherwise, there would be a difference between two columns. Depending on whether the elemental energy or global energy is under investigation, users can flexibly choose the columns to be compared.

docs.title: Eccentricity
docs.text:
This page discusses the eccentricity of a section.

Consider the following T-section with $\(b_f=7.04\)$, $\(t_f=0.59\)$, $\(b_w=11.31\)$ and $\(t_w=0.43\)$. It is WT12X31 section in the AISC table.

The barycentre can be computed as

\[ \begin{split} y=&\dfrac{b_wt_w(b_w/2)+b_ft_f(b_w+t_f/2)}{b_wt_w+b_ft_f}\\ =&\dfrac{11.31^2\times0.43/2+7.04\times0.59\times(11.31+0.59/2)}{11.31\times0.43+7.04\times0.59}\\ =&8.3958 \end{split} \]

The eccentricity is then the difference between the default origin (centroid of web) and the barycentre.

\[ e=8.3958-11.31/2=2.7408. \]

Or simply,

\[ e=\dfrac{7.04\times0.59\times(11.31/2+0.59/2)}{11.31\times0.43+7.04\times0.59}\\ =2.7408. \]

If the default trivial eccentricity is used, then axial loading will lead to transverse displacement. See the following example.

Text Only
node 1 0 0
node 2 1 0
material Elastic1D 1 1
section US2D WT12X31 1 1 1 10 0
element B21 1 1 2 1
fix2 1 E 1
displacement 1 0 1 1 2 ! apply axial load
step static 1
set ini_step_size 1
analyze
# Node 2:
# Coordinate:
#   1.0000e+00  0.0000e+00
# Displacement:
#   1.0000e+00 -6.2092e-02 -1.2418e-01 <--- transverse displacement and rotation
# Resistance:
#   5.9478e+00 -1.3410e-14 -1.7171e-14
peek node 2
exit

Manually setting the eccentricity removes the extra bending. It needs to be moved down by $\(2.7408\)$ so that the barycentre is at the origin.

Text Only
node 1 0 0
node 2 1 0
material Elastic1D 1 1
section US2D WT12X31 1 1 1 10 -2.740844414 ! manually set eccentricity
element B21 1 1 2 1
fix2 1 E 1
displacement 1 0 1 1 2
step static 1
set ini_step_size 1
analyze
# Node 2:
# Coordinate:
#   1.0000e+00  0.0000e+00
# Displacement:
#   1.0000e+00 -1.2963e-11 -2.5926e-11 <--- no more transverse displacement and rotation
# Resistance:
#   9.0169e+00 -1.9722e-31  8.8818e-16
peek node 2
exit

The axial rigidity matches the theoretical value with area being $\(A=11.31\times0.43+7.04\times0.59=9.0169\)$.

The flexural rigidity can be obtained by applying a transverse loading.

Text Only
node 1 0 0
node 2 1 0
material Elastic1D 1 1
section US2D WT12X31 1 1 1 10 -2.740844414
element B21 1 1 2 1
fix2 1 E 1
displacement 1 0 1 2 2 ! apply unit transverse load
step static 1
set ini_step_size 1
analyze
# Node 2:
# Coordinate:
#   1.0000e+00  0.0000e+00
# Displacement:
#  -5.6617e-10  1.0000e+00  1.5000e+00
# Resistance:
#  -1.5586e-15  3.9382e+02 -7.1057e-15
peek node 2
exit

From the AISC table, the moment of inertia is $\(I=131\)$, then $\(3EI=393\approx393.82\)$.

By the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia when the section is placed at the centre of the web is

\[ I=I_z+Ad^2=131+9.0169\times2.7408^2=199. \]

It can be further verified by applying a moment while restraining the axial displacement.

Text Only
node 1 0 0
node 2 1 0
material Elastic1D 1 1
section US2D WT12X31 1 1 1 10 0
element B21 1 1 2 1
fix2 1 E 1
fix2 2 1 2 ! fix axial displacement
displacement 1 0 1 3 2 ! apply unit moment
step static 1
set ini_step_size 1
analyze
# Node 2:
# Coordinate:
#   1.0000e+00  0.0000e+00
# Displacement:
#   0.0000e+00  5.0000e-01  1.0000e+00
# Resistance:
#   2.4714e+01  3.1264e-13  1.9901e+02 <--- moment of inertia
peek node 2
exit

This manual adjustment of eccentricity exists since it is beneficial when it comes to creating complex sections of basic shapes.

But when analysing simple sections alone, it is desired to place the section at its barycenter. This is not a problem for symmetric sections, but for asymmetric sections, the default eccentricity would cause unwanted results.

There are US2DC and US3DC available, which automatically adjust the eccentricity so that all forces are applied at the barycenter.

docs.title: Validation EU Designation¶
docs.text:
All HEA, HEB, HEM, IPE, UB, UC and UBP section designations are supported.

The reference values are the tabulated EN 10365:2017 section properties.

docs.title: EU
docs.text:
Eurocode 3 Sections

See Eccentricity for more details.

Text Only
section EU2D (1) (2) (3) [4] [5] [6]
# (1) string, designation
# (2) int, unique tag
# (3) int, material model tag
# [4] double, scale, default: 1.0
# [5] int, number of integration points, default: 6
# [6] double, eccentricity, default: 0.0

section EU3D (1) (2) (3) [4] [5] [6] [7]
# (1) string, designation
# (2) int, unique tag
# (3) int, material model tag
# [4] double, scale, default: 1.0
# [5] int, number of integration points, default: 6
# [6] double, eccentricity of y axis, default: 0.0
# [7] double, eccentricity of z axis, default: 0.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. By default, millimeter is used as length unit, if users want to switch to another unit, set scale to corresponding values. For example, to use meter, scale=0.001, to use inch, scale=1/25.4=0.03937007874.
  2. Check validation for accuracy validations.

docs.title: Adjusted Sections
docs.text:
The nominal EU registry uses the published nominal dimensions of each shape. The rectangular I-section idealization ignores root fillets and flange taper, so the area, moments of inertia and section moduli computed from the nominal geometry differ from the values tabulated in EN 10365:2017.

The adjusted registry keeps the same designations but replaces the nominal dimensions with effective dimensions optimized against the tabulated section properties. Use the A suffix to select the adjusted registry.

Adjusted EU
section EU2DA (1) (2) (3) [4] [5] [6]
section EU3DA (1) (2) (3) [4] [5] [6] [7]
# (1) string, designation
# (2) int, unique tag
# (3) int, material model tag
# [4] double, scale, default: 1.0
# [5] int, number of integration points, default: 6
# [6] double, eccentricity (eccentricity of y axis for 3D), default: 0.0
# [7] double, eccentricity of z axis, default: 0.0

The arguments are identical to the corresponding EU2D and EU3D commands. For example:

Text Only
section EU2DA HEA200 1 1
section EU3DA IPE300 2 1
section EU2DA UB203X133X25 3 1
section EU3DA UBP305X305X110 4 1

docs.title: What Is Changed
docs.text:
• The section properties are extracted from the Dlubal cross-section database (HEA, HEB, HEM and IPE and UB, UC and UBP), both EN 10365:2017, ArcelorMittal 2018.
  • eu.csv contains the properties of all HEA, HEB, HEM, IPE, UB, UC and UBP designations. It stores the nominal dimensions h, b, tw, tf, the root radius r1, and the tabulated properties A, I_strong, I_weak, W_strong, W_weak, Wpl_strong and Wpl_weak. The strong/weak labels avoid the EN y/z axis naming, where y is the strong axis.
  • eu_registry_generator.py adjusts the flange width, flange thickness, web depth and web thickness so that the rectangular idealization reproduces A, Ix, Iy, Zx and Zy. Equal flanges are kept equal.
  • Every adjusted dimension stays within 10 % of its nominal value.
  • The nominal EU2D/EU3D registries use the published nominal geometry.
  • Dlubal reports the strong axis as y and the weak axis as z; in suanPan the strong axis is x.

docs.title: What Is Achieved
docs.text:
• For all 290 HEA, HEB, HEM, IPE, UB, UC and UBP sections, the error of the area and of the strong-axis properties (A, Ix, Zx) is below 0.8 %; it is below 0.4 % for the UB, UC and UBP series. The largest weak-axis error (Iy, Zy) is 1.0 %.
  • The overall maximum property error is 1.0 %, compared with errors of several percent when the nominal dimensions are used directly.
  • The adjusted dimensions remain close to the nominal geometry: the section depth changes by less than 1.5 % and the flange width by less than 3 %.

The adjusted dimensions are effective dimensions for the idealization, not a replacement for the EN 10365 geometry. The computed properties still depend on the number of integration points; see the validation for the numerical accuracy of the section integration.

docs.title: Validation NZ Designation¶
docs.text:
All AS/NZS 3679.1 UB and UC section designations are supported.

The reference values are the tabulated AS/NZS 3679.1 section properties.

docs.title: NZ
docs.text:
NZ Code Sections

Sections in accordance with AS/NZ standards are available in both 2D and 3D applications.

See Eccentricity for more details.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
To define a section, analysts can use the following commands.

NZ
section NZ2D (1) (2) (3) [4] [5] [6]
# (1) string, designation
# (2) int, unique tag
# (3) int, material model tag
# [4] double, scale, default: 1.0
# [5] int, number of integration points, default: 6
# [6] double, eccentricity, default: 0.0

section NZ3D (1) (2) (3) [4] [5] [6] [7]
# (1) string, designation
# (2) int, unique tag
# (3) int, material model tag
# [4] double, scale, default: 1.0
# [5] int, number of integration points, default: 6
# [6] double, eccentricity of y axis, default: 0.0
# [7] double, eccentricity of z axis, default: 0.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. By default, millimeter is used as length unit, if users want to switch to another unit, set scale to corresponding values. For example, to use meter, scale=0.001, to use inch, scale=1/25.4=0.03937007874.
  2. For 2D sections, the number of integration points is set to two using Gauss quadrature for flanges in I-sections.
  3. For 3D sections, along web/flange thickness, one integration point is used. Along flange width and web height, the same number of integration points is used as defined by user.

There will be discrepancies between design section properties and numerical section properties. Use with caution and check the validation.

docs.title: Adjusted Sections
docs.text:
The nominal NZ registry uses the published nominal dimensions of each shape. The rectangular I-section idealization ignores root fillets and flange taper, so the area, moments of inertia and section moduli computed from the nominal geometry differ from the values tabulated in AS/NZS 3679.1.

The adjusted registry keeps the same designations but replaces the nominal dimensions with effective dimensions optimized against the tabulated section properties. Use the A suffix to select the adjusted registry.

Adjusted NZ
section NZ2DA (1) (2) (3) [4] [5] [6]
section NZ3DA (1) (2) (3) [4] [5] [6] [7]
# (1) string, designation
# (2) int, unique tag
# (3) int, material model tag
# [4] double, scale, default: 1.0
# [5] int, number of integration points, default: 6
# [6] double, eccentricity (eccentricity of y axis for 3D), default: 0.0
# [7] double, eccentricity of z axis, default: 0.0

The arguments are identical to the corresponding NZ2D and NZ3D commands. For example:

Text Only
section NZ2DA 610UB113 1 1
section NZ3DA 310UC137 2 1

docs.title: What Is Changed
docs.text:
• The section properties are extracted from the Dlubal cross-section database (UB and UC, AS/NZS 3679.1, Tung Ho Steel) and stored in nz.csv.
  • The CSV stores the nominal dimensions h, b, tw, tf, the root radius r1, and the tabulated properties A, I_strong, I_weak, W_strong, W_weak, Wpl_strong and Wpl_weak. The strong/weak labels avoid the AS/NZS x/y axis naming, where x is the strong axis.
  • eu_registry_generator.py adjusts the flange width, flange thickness, web depth and web thickness so that the rectangular idealization reproduces A, Ix, Iy, Zx and Zy. Equal flanges are kept equal.
  • Every adjusted dimension stays within 10 % of its nominal value.
  • The nominal NZ2D/NZ3D registries are unchanged and still use the published nominal geometry.
  • The adjusted registry contains the 41 AS/NZS 3679.1 UB and UC designations listed below. NZ2DA/NZ3DA report an error for other NZ shapes, which remain available through the nominal commands.
  • For six UB sizes (310UB32.0, 310UB40.4, 310UB46.2, 360UB44.7, 360UB50.7 and 360UB56.7) the manufacturer series reports plastic moduli that are inconsistent with its own elastic values. The tabulated values of the generic AS/NZS 3679.1 series are used for these six sizes instead.

docs.title: What Is Achieved
docs.text:
• For all 41 UB and UC sections, the error of the area and of the strong-axis properties (A, Ix, Zx) is below 0.6 % for the UB series and below 0.95 % for the UC series. The largest weak-axis error (Iy, Zy) is below 0.8 %.
  • The adjusted dimensions remain close to the nominal geometry: the section depth changes by less than 1.5 %, the flange width by less than 1.5 % and the flange thickness by less than 4.5 %.

The adjusted dimensions are effective dimensions for the idealization, not a replacement for the AS/NZS 3679.1 geometry. The computed properties still depend on the number of integration points.

docs.title: Validation US Designation¶
docs.text: In this page, we validate the section properties of some US designations. All W, S, M, WT, ST, MT, HP, HSS designations, which are compiled and well documented in the AISC Shapes Database v16.0, are included.

docs.title: Some Utilities¶
docs.text: The spreadsheet is loaded directly via the url.

docs.title: Analysis Template¶
docs.text:
Next, we define the function to run the analysis and extract the result.

The following is the template model file that will be used. A few things to note:

  1. The material is assumed to be elastic with a unit elastic modulus.
  2. The default integration scheme is used for each designation.
  3. A unit displacement load is applied to axial, strong axis bending and weak axis bending.
  4. The US3DC category is used, it automatically recentre the section to its barycentre if it is not symmetric.

docs.title: Extract Results¶
docs.text: To extract the data, we process the output.

docs.title: Collect All Sections¶
docs.text: We can now iterate over all sections.

docs.title: Area¶
docs.text:
In general, the area can be relatively accurately computed. However, as all those sections are internally modelled by three flat pieces, the root fillet cannot be accounted for. As a result, the numerical area is often smaller than the reference value.

Some very light M shapes cannot be well approximated.

docs.title: Strong Axis Bending¶
docs.text: Some very heavy T sections tend to have poor strong axis moment of inertia. In this shapes, the thickness of flange accounts for a significant portion of the overall depth. The normal stress in the flange presents gradient. In the meantime, there is only one layer of integration points along the thickness of flange, which is not accurate enough in this case.

docs.title: Weak Axis Bending¶
docs.text: The tapered shapes tend to have more material towards the center, as a result, the weak axis moment of inertia is smaller. It is modelled by a flat rectangle in numerical models, this overestimate the moment of inertia, mainly for S and ST shapes.

docs.title: Automation Utilities¶
docs.text: The following is the script to generate autocompletion. Readers can safely ignore it.

docs.title: AISC
docs.text:
A collection of W, M, S, HP, WT, MT, ST sections are predefined using inch as default length unit.

See Eccentricity for more details.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
To define a section, users can use the following commands.

US
section US2D (1) (2) (3) [4] [5] [6]
# (1) string, designation
# (2) int, unique tag
# (3) int, material model tag
# [4] double, scale, default: 1.0
# [5] int, number of integration points along web height, default: 6
# [6] double, eccentricity, default: 0.0

section US3D (1) (2) (3) [4] [5] [6] [7]
# (1) string, designation
# (2) int, unique tag
# (3) int, material model tag
# [4] double, scale, default: 1.0
# [5] int, number of integration points along web height and flange width, default: 6
# [6] double, eccentricity of y axis, default: 0.0
# [7] double, eccentricity of z axis, default: 0.0

[available from v3.2]

Some T-sections are placed at the centre of the web, which is not always desired. Use US2DC and US3DC to automatically recenter the section to its barycenter.

Text Only
section US2DC (1) (2) (3) [4] [5]
section US3DC (1) (2) (3) [4] [5]
# (1) string, designation
# (2) int, unique tag
# (3) int, material model tag
# [4] double, scale, default: 1.0
# [5] int, number of integration points along web height (and flange width for 3D), default: 6

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. By default, inch is used as length unit, if users want to switch to another unit, set scale to corresponding values. For example, to use millimeter, scale=25.4.
  2. For 2D sections, the number of integration points is set to two using Gauss quadrature for flange.
  3. For 3D sections, along web/flange thickness, one integration point is used. Along flange width and web height, the same number of integration points is used as defined by user.

There will be discrepancies between design section properties and numerical section properties. Use with caution and check the validation.

docs.title: Adjusted Sections
docs.text:
The nominal US registry uses the published nominal dimensions of each shape. For rolled shapes this idealization ignores fillets, flange taper and other details, so the area, moments of inertia and section moduli computed from the nominal geometry can differ noticeably from the values tabulated by AISC.

The adjusted registry uses the same designations but replaces the nominal dimensions with effective dimensions optimized against the tabulated AISC properties. The A suffix selects the adjusted registry and the AC suffix combines the adjustment with automatic recentering.

Adjusted US
section US2DA (1) (2) (3) [4] [5] [6]
section US3DA (1) (2) (3) [4] [5] [6] [7]
section US2DAC (1) (2) (3) [4] [5]
section US3DAC (1) (2) (3) [4] [5]
# (1) string, designation
# (2) int, unique tag
# (3) int, material model tag
# [4] double, scale, default: 1.0
# [5] int, number of integration points along web height (and flange width for 3D), default: 6
# [6] double, eccentricity (eccentricity of y axis for 3D), default: 0.0
# [7] double, eccentricity of z axis, default: 0.0

The arguments are identical to the corresponding US2D, US3D, US2DC and US3DC commands. For example:

Text Only
section US2DA W14X90 1 1
section US3DAC WT12X31 2 1

docs.title: What Is Changed
docs.text:
• The adjusted registries are generated from the AISC Shapes Database v16.0 with section_optimizer.py.
  • The optimizer scales the dimensions of the rectangular I-section, T-section and hollow-section idealizations so that the computed properties follow the tabulated values of A, Ix, Iy, Zx and Zy.
  • For the M, S and ST families, the dimensions are allowed to move by at most 7 % from the nominal values. This is enough to keep all strong-axis properties (A, Ix, Zx) within 5 % for every section.
  • The weak-axis properties (Iy, Zy) are also targets, but they are allowed to exceed 5 % for the two smallest ST shapes, ST2X3.85 and ST1.5X2.85, where the rectangular idealization is too coarse to fit all five properties at once.
  • The nominal US2D/US3D registries are unchanged. They still use the published nominal geometry.

docs.title: What Is Achieved
docs.text:
• Axial stiffness, strong-axis bending stiffness and strong-axis plastic capacity are much closer to the AISC tabulated values than with the nominal dimensions.
  • The adjusted M/S/ST dimensions stay within 7 % of the nominal geometry, so overall section depth and width remain close to the designated shape.
  • The strong-axis property error is at most about 4.1 % over all M/S/ST sections, and the weak-axis error is at most about 5.7 %, with only the two noted ST shapes above 5 %.
  • The choice between nominal and adjusted sections is explicit: use US2D/US3D when the exact published geometry is required, and US2DA/US3DA when the tabulated section properties are more important.

The adjusted dimensions are effective dimensions for the idealization, not a replacement for the AISC geometry. The computed properties still depend on the number of integration points; see the validation for the numerical accuracy of the section integration.

docs.title: Box2D
docs.text: 2D Box Section

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Box2D
section Box2D (1) (2) (3) (4) (5) [6] [7]
# (1) int, unique section tag
# (2) double, width
# (3) double, height
# (4) double, thickness
# (5) int, material tag
# [6] int, number of integration points, default: 6
# [7] double, eccentricity/location, default: 0.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
The eccentricity is measured from the centre of the section.

The width and height are measured from midline to midline.

Under the hood, the section is computed as an I-section. The integration scheme applies.

docs.title: CircularHollow2D
docs.text:
2D Hollow Circular Section

The radius should be the outer radius, which shall be half of the overall diameter.

# (2) double, radius
# (3) double, thickness
# (4) int, material tag
# [5] int, number of integration points for half circle, default: 6
# [6] double, eccentricity/location, default: 0.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: The eccentricity is measured from the centre of the section.

# (8) int, material tag
# [9] int, number of integration points for flanges, default: 6
# [10] double, eccentricity/location, default: 0.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. Section dimensions are:
  2. (2) left flange height
  3. (3) left flange thickness
  4. (4) right flange height
  5. (5) right flange thickness
  6. (6) web width
  7. (7) web thickness

Two integration points are used for web. The user assigned number of integration points is used for flanges.

The eccentricity is measured from the centre of the web/flanges. If the left and right flanges have different sizes, the default trivial eccentricity will lead to extra bending moments when the section is subjected to axial force. Eccentricity can be manually adjusted.

docs.text:

  3. If the web thickness exceeds 10% of the larger flange width, the web will use two integration point layers through its thickness.

See Eccentricity for more details.

docs.title: NM2D2
docs.text: $\(N\)\(-\)\(M\)$ Interaction Inelastic Section (Linear Hardening)

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. 10.1061/JSENDH.STENG-12176

docs.title: Option One
docs.text:
NM2D2
section NM2D2 (1) (2...9)
# (1) int, unique section tag
# (2) double, EA
# (3) double, EI
# (4) double, yielding axial force
# (5) double, yielding strong axis moment
# (6) double, c
# (7) double, isotropic hardening parameter H
# (8) double, kinematic hardening parameter K
# (9) double, linear density

If the NM2D2 section is defined by using the above command, it is assumed that the $\(N\)\(-\)\(M\)$ interaction surface is defined as follows.

\[ f=1.15p^2+m_s^2+3.67p^2m_s^2-c \]

where $\(p\)$ and $\(m_s\)$ are normalised axial force and moment (about the strong axis). This surface is suitable for I-sections.

docs.title: Option Two
docs.text:
One may wish to customise the surface by assigning different weights and orders; it is possible by using the following syntax.

Text Only
section NM2D2 (1) (2...9) [(10) (11) (12) ...]
# (1) int, unique section tag
# (2) double, EA
# (3) double, EI
# (4) double, yielding axial force
# (5) double, yielding strong axis moment
# (6) double, d
# (7) double, isotropic hardening parameter H
# (8) double, kinematic hardening parameter K
# (9) double, linear density
# (10) double, a_i
# (11) double, b_i
# (12) double, c_i

In the above command, parameters (10), (11) and (12) form a triplet and can be appended as many groups as the analyst wishes. The surface is assumed to possess the following form,

\[ f=\sum_{i=1}^na_ip^{b_i}m_s^{c_i}-d. \]

For example, the previous surface $\(f=1.15p^2+m_s^2+3.67p^2m_s^2-c\)$ can be equivalently expressed with the second syntax as follows.

Text Only
section NM2D2 (1) (2...9) 1.15 2. 0. 1. 0. 2. 3.67 2. 2.

The only validation implemented is the number of triplets. The command takes $\(3n\)$ parameters and interprets them accordingly. Please make sure the definition is correct.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
The true hardening ratio is defined as

\[ \dfrac{H+K}{1+H+K}, \]

given that $\(H\)$ and $\(K\)$ are hardening ratios based on plastic strain.

docs.title: Output Type
docs.text:
This model supports the following additional history variables to be recorded.

variable label physical meaning YF yielding flag (vector of size 2)

docs.title: SectionNM
docs.text: $\(N\)\(-\)\(M\)$ Interaction Abstract Section

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. 10.1061/JSENDH.STENG-12176
  2. 10.1007/978-94-007-6573-3_3
  3. 10.1002/nme.1620371506

Please note the formulation is based on the first reference, which is a revised version of the one shown in the last two references.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
Strictly speaking, the SectionNM is not a section, as a conventional section takes sectional elongation and curvature as input and computes sectional force and moment as output. The SectionNM takes elemental deformation and resistance (which are local quantities of two end nodes) and directly computes the force and moment. Loosely speaking, the SectionNM is a special model that accounts for two end sections simultaneously.

According to 10.1061/JSENDH.STENG-12176, the whole model can be implemented at the element level. It is chosen to separate the model into the element part (NMB* elements) and the section part (NM2D* and NM3D* sections) for better code organisation.

Apart from the provided sections, other interaction surfaces can be defined.

One can define a derived class based on, for example, SurfaceNM2D, and implement methods.

C++
[[nodiscard]] double compute_sf(const vec&, const vec&) const;
[[nodiscard]] vec compute_dsf(const vec&, const vec&) const;
[[nodiscard]] mat compute_ddsf(const vec&, const vec&) const;

All methods take the normalised shifted resistance $\(\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{\beta}\)$ and equivalent plastic strain $\(\alpha\)$ as input where $\(\mathbf{q}\)$ is the normalised nodal resistance and $\(\mathbf{\beta}\)$ is the back resistance, which is similar to the concept of back stress.

docs.title: Cell3DOS
docs.text: Basic Building Block for 3D OS Section

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Distributed plasticity analysis of steel building structural systems

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Cell3DOS
section Cell3DOS (1) (2) (3) (4) (5) (6) [7] [8]
# (1) int, unique section tag
# (2) double, area
# (3) double, sectional coordinate
# (4) double, py
# (5) double, pz
# (6) int, material tag
# [7] double, eccentricity/location along y axis, default: 0.0
# [8] double, eccentricity/location along z axis, default: 0.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
The parameter (3) is the warping function $\(\omega\)$.

The parameters (4) and (5) are partial derivatives of the warping function $\(\omega\)$, namely, $\(\frac{\partial \omega}{\partial y}\)$ and $\(\frac{\partial \omega}{\partial z}\)$.

The attached material needs to be an OS material. Use a wrapper, for example, OS146 (for 3D host material) and OS146S (for 1D host material with linear elastic shear response).

docs.title: Fibre3DOS
docs.text: 3D OS Fibre Section

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Distributed plasticity analysis of steel building structural systems
  2. Analysis and Design of Elastic Beams: Computational Methods

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Fibre3DOS
section Fibre3DOS (1) [(2)...]
# (1) int, unique section tag
# [(2)...] int, associated section tags

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
The associated sections need to be OS sections.

The section takes twelve quantities from the parent element, namely,

\[ \begin{bmatrix} u'&v'&w'&v''&w''&\phi&\phi'&\phi''&\theta_{z,i}&\theta_{z,j}&\theta_{y,i}&\theta_{y,j} \end{bmatrix} \]

Note

All quantities ($\(u\)$, $\(v\)$, $\(w\)$ and $\(\phi\)\() are measured about the reference axis (\)\(y=z=0\)$). Any offset/shift should be directly defined via section composition.

Then strain components are determined by the following equations:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \varepsilon_{11}\\ \gamma_{12}\\ \gamma_{13} \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} u'-yv''-zw''+\omega\phi''+\left(zv''-yw''\right)\phi+\dfrac{1}{2}(y^2+z^2)\left(\phi'\right) ^2+\dfrac{1}{60}\mathbf{\theta}^\mathrm{T}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{\theta}\\ \left(\dfrac{\partial\omega}{\partial{}y}-z\right)\phi'\\ \left(\dfrac{\partial\omega}{\partial{}z}+y\right)\phi' \end{bmatrix} \]

The normal strain is defined according to Alemdar's thesis (Eq. 7.63). The shear strains are defined according to Pilkey's book (Eq. 5.3).

Alemdar's thesis and its derivatives use $\(\gamma=-2n\phi'\)$ to define the shear strain. This definition is acceptable for thin-walled sections, where a clear physical implication of parameter $\(n\)$ can be found. For arbitrary sections, such a definition would be problematic. We use a general definition instead. Then there are two shear components instead of one. The remaining three strain components are zero. The wrapper OS146 can be used to prepare compatible materials.

docs.title: AICN
docs.text:
The AICN solver implements a damped Newton method.

arXiv:2211.00140

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
AICN
solver AICN (1) [2]
# (1) int, unique solver tag
# [2] double, approx. length, default: 1.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. AICN is an alternative to the Newton solver.

For example usage, see this example.

docs.title: BFGS
docs.text: The BFGS solver uses the rank-two update algorithm BFGS. Alternatively, the limited memory version can also be switched on.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
The implementation is based on Algorithm 7.4.

  1. Numerical Optimization

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
BFGS
solver BFGS (1)
solver LBFGS (1) [2]
# (1) int, unique solver tag
# [2] int, number of steps stored, default: 20

docs.title: Details and Limitations
docs.text:
The global stiffness matrix is assembled in the very first iteration of each sub-step. Subsequent iterations use this matrix as the initial Hessian.

Since BFGS possesses a super-linear convergence rate, the overall performance should be better than that of the modified Newton method.

Regardless of whether LBFGS is used, the maximum number of iterations will be limited to the size of the problem.

There is no support for constraints implemented via the Lagrange multiplier method.

Theoretically, BFGS only works on symmetric positive definite systems. The algorithm will eventually fail if the system is not positive definite. Thus, it cannot be used in problems that exhibit material softening, snap-back, snap-through, etc. However, the solver itself does not validate the type of systems given.

docs.title: MPDC
docs.text: Multiple Points Displacement Control

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
MPDC
solver MPDC (1)
solver DisplacementControl (1)
# (1) int, unique solver tag

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: 1. The MPDC solver is automatically enabled if the current step has an active displacement load.

docs.title: Newton
docs.text: The Newton solver defines a classic (modified) Newton-Raphson solver.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Newton
solver Newton (1)
solver modifiedNewton (1)
solver mNewton (1)
# (1) int, unique solver tag

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The modified Newton method only assembles tangent stiffness at the beginning of each sub-step. Automatic stepping can be enabled to obtain optimised computational workload.
  2. The Aitken acceleration is automatically enabled in the modified Newton method.

docs.title: Ramm
docs.text:
Arc Length Algorithm Using Ramm's Approach

Ramm's version of the arc length algorithm is implemented. This solver can only be used in solving static problems.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Ramm
solver Ramm (1)
# (1) int, unique solver tag

The step size in an arc-length analysis is now the arc length. One can use the following to control stepping strategy.

Text Only
set ini_step_size (1)
set min_step_size (1)
set max_step_size (1)
# (1) double, step size (arc length)

set fixed_step_size (1)
# (1) bool, flag to indicate whether to fix the arc length

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. A proper arc length shall be manually input to achieve an efficient analysis.
  2. Often the arc length is allowed to change depending on the smoothness of the turning point.
  3. If the arc length is not fixed, a positive minimum/maximum arc length (step size) will kick in to prevent the arc length from being too small/large.
  4. Any non-positive values for the minimum/maximum arc length will be ignored.

A good overview of the method and its implementation details can be found in Crisfield's book (ISBN: 9780471929567), see Chapter 9.

Solvers for symmetric storage often require the target matrix to be positive definite. This is not the case in arc-length related applications, although it can still be used for problems in which the tangent stiffness is positive definite. Thus, as a rule of thumb, one may need to switch off symm_mat.

Text Only
set symm_mat 0

If positive definiteness is known to be guaranteed, symmetric storage can also be used.

For general cases, the (sign of) determinant of the tangent stiffness is required to identify turning points. Not all solvers support the computation of determinant.

docs.title: Without MPI
docs.text:
Only LAPACK based solvers can be used. Thus, one needs to use the following settings. Note they are all default settings thus do not need to be explicitly set. The point is do not choose something else.

Text Only
set symm_mat 0
set band_mat 1
set sparse_mat 0
set system_solver LAPACK

docs.title: With MPI
docs.text:
Only the MUMPS solver is able to compute the determinant. ScaLAPACK based solvers do not support inspection of factorization thus cannot provide an efficient way of computing determinant. Thus, one needs to enable sparse storage and choose the MUMPS solver.

Text Only
set sparse_mat 1
set system_solver MUMPS

docs.title: Prior to v3.2.0
docs.text:
For versions prior to v3.2.0, the syntax is as follows. Only one single DoF is permitted to be controlled. It is directly defined in the step command.

ArcLength
step ArcLength (1) (2) (3) (4)
# (1) int, unique step tag
# (2) int, reference node tag
# (3) int, reference dof tag
# (4) double, reference magnitude of applied load

docs.title: v3.2.0 and later
docs.text:
For versions v3.2.0 and later, the syntax is as follows. The reference load is no longer defined in the step command. Instead, it is defined by the RefForce command.

Text Only
step ArcLength (1)
# (1) int, unique step tag

docs.title: Arc-length Control
docs.text:
The step size in an arc-length analysis is now the arc length. One can use the following to control stepping strategy.

Text Only
set ini_step_size (1)
set min_step_size (1)
set max_step_size (1)
# (1) double, step size (arc length)

set fixed_step_size (1)
# (1) bool, flag to indicate whether to fix the arc length

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: 1. A Ramm solver with default parameters is automatically enabled if no valid Ramm solver is defined. Not all storage schemes are supported; please check Ramm documentation.

docs.title: Buckle
docs.text: The Buckle step defines a linear buckling analysis.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Buckle
step Buckle (1)
step Buckling (1)
# (1) int, unique step tag

docs.title: Implicit Dynamics System
docs.text: The implicit dynamics system uses displacement as the primary variable.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Dynamic
step dynamic (1) [2]
step implicitdynamic (1) [2]
# (1) int, unique step tag
# [2] double, time period, default: 1.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. Displacement control solver MPDC is automatically enabled if a displacement load is active.
  2. The Newmark is automatically enabled if there is no valid integrator defined.

docs.title: Explicit Dynamics System
docs.text:
The explicit dynamics system uses acceleration as the primary variable.

All displacement based loads/constraints cannot be applied.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Dynamic
step explicitdynamic (1) [2]
# (1) int, unique step tag
# [2] double, time period, default: 1.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: 1. The Tchamwa with spectral radius of $\(0.8\)$ is automatically enabled if there is no valid integrator defined.

docs.title: Frequency
docs.text:
The (generalized) eigenvalue problem is handled in the Frequency step. To define a valid step, please use the following command.

Text Only
step frequency (1) [2] [3]
# (1) int, unique step tag
# [2] int, number of eigen modes to be solved, default: 1
# [3] string, eigenvalue type, default: s

To successfully run an eigen analysis, the system shall be symmetric, otherwise complex eigenvalues are computed. This typically requires the stiffness matrix to be symmetric. Besides, it must have

  1. a positive definite stiffness matrix,
  2. a semi-positive definite mass matrix.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The symmetric banded storage uses the _pbsv solver which only accepts a symmetric positive definite banded matrix. If the Frequency fails to compute the required eigen modes, please use other storage schemes.
  2. The computed eigenvalue is the eigenvalue of the system. In the field of structural dynamics, it is $\(\omega^2\)$. The (angular) frequency and period can be computed accordingly.
  3. The constrained (generalized) eigenvalue problems cannot be handled when the constraints are implemented via the Lagrange multiplier method. If the system contains constraints, users shall make sure they are applied via the penalty function method.

docs.title: Modal Properties
docs.text:
The eigenanalysis itself stores the eigenvalues and eigenvectors in the global factory. To write frequencies, mode shapes, participation factors, effective modal masses and modal elastic forces to an HDF5 file, use the Modal recorder.

Text Only
recorder 1 hdf5 Modal U1
step frequency 1 10
analyze
save recorder 1

docs.title: FEAST Solver
docs.text:
By default, the ARPACK solver is used to solve the generalized eigen problem.

The FEAST Eigenvalue Solver can also be used. To switch, one can use

Text Only
solver FEAST (1) (2) (3) [4]
# (1) int, unique solver tag
# (2) int, number of eigen modes
# (3) double, centre
# [4] double, radius, default: centre

Currently, the FEAST solver can be applied to full, banded and sparse storage. For banded storage, it is necessary to use the SPIKE solver.

Text Only
set system_solver SPIKE

For the given centre $\(c\)$ and radius $\(r\)$, the FEAST solver seeks eigenvalues within the bracket $\([c-r,c+r]\)$. If the radius is not assigned, it defaults to $\(c\)$, thus the bracket becomes $\([0,2c]\)$.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Consider a massless elastic cantilever beam with lumped end mass. Assume the length is $\(L=2.84\)$, the elastic modulus is $\(E=94.13\)$, the moment of inertia is $\(I=1.34\)$ and the lumped mass is $\(M=5.76\)$ so that

\[ \omega^2=\dfrac{3EI}{ML^3}=\dfrac{3\times94.13\times1.34}{5.76\times2.84^3}=2.8680. \] Text Only
node 1 0 0
node 2 0 2.84
material Elastic1D 1 94.13
element EB21 1 1 2 1 1.34 1
mass 2 2 5.76 1
fix 1 E 1
recorder 1 hdf5 Eigen
step frequency 1 1
analyze
peek eigenvalue
exit

The output is

|  /  \      |  \          FEM framework (64-bit)  |
|  \__       |__/  __   __          Acrux (0.1.0)  |
|     \ |  | |    |  \ |  |                        |
|  \__/ |__| |    |__X |  |     maintained by tlc  |
|                             all rights reserved  |
+--------------------------------------------------+

Eigenvalues:
   2.8680

Finished in 0.005 seconds.

docs.title: Optimization
docs.text: Structural Optimization Step

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Optimization
step Optimization (1) [2]
# (1) int, unique step tag
# [2] double, time period, default: 1.0

It shall be noted that all previously defined steps will be analyzed by the end of the ESO step.

docs.title: Per Step Configurations
docs.text:
As mentioned in Structure, the commands used between two steps belong to the first step. This means the following.

Text Only
# first step of duration 4.0
step static 1 4.0

# anything defined here belongs to the first step 
# including convergers, integrators, solvers, solver settings, etc.

# second step of duration 4.0
step static 2 4.0

# anything defined here belongs to the first step 
# including convergers, integrators, solvers, solver settings, etc.

# maybe more steps
step static 3 4.0

Similar to ABAQUS, one can use different settings for different steps. For example, for the following snippet,

Text Only
# first step of duration 4.0
step static 1 4.0

set ini_step_size .1
set fixed_step_size true

converger RelIncreDisp 1 1E-10 3 1

# second step of duration 4.0
step static 2 4.0

set ini_step_size 1.0
set fixed_step_size false

converger AbsIncreDisp 2 1E-8 10 1

one can interpret the above as follows.

  1. Step 1
    1. Use an initial step size of $\(0.1\)$.
    2. Fix the step size to $\(0.1\)$. Since the duration is $\(4.0\)$, the total number of substeps is $\(40\)$.
    3. Use a relative displacement increment RelIncreDisp converger with a tolerance of $\(10^{-10}\)$.
  2. Step 2
    1. Use an initial step size of $\(1.0\)$.
    2. Allow the step size to vary. The algorithm would automatically adjust the step size to satisfy the convergence criteria.
    3. Use an absolute displacement increment AbsIncreDisp converger with a tolerance of $\(10^{-8}\)$.

docs.title: Inheriting from Previous Steps
docs.text:
For convergers, integrators and solvers, if there are no corresponding objects defined in the current step, the objects of the previous step are inherited if the previous step defines them, otherwise default ones will be used.

Text Only
# first step of duration 4.0
step static 1 4.0

# a valid converger is defined in the first step
converger RelIncreDisp 1 1E-10 3 1

# second step of duration 4.0
step static 2 4.0

# some other settings

Since there is no converger defined in the second step, the converger defined in the first step will be used in the second step.

Text Only
# first step of duration 4.0
step static 1 4.0

# second step of duration 4.0
step static 2 4.0

# a valid converger is defined in the second step
converger RelIncreDisp 1 1E-10 3 1

For the above, since there is no converger defined in the first step, the default converger will be used in the first step. The converger defined in the second step will not affect the first step.

Warning

The solver settings are not inherited. They must be defined in each step. This is because if two steps use the same solver settings, it's likely that it is possible to combine two steps into one step. If two steps are intended, it is likely that the solver settings are different.

docs.title: Static
docs.text:
To define a static analysis, the Static step shall be used.

Text Only
step static (1) [2]
# (1) int, unique step tag
# [2] double, step length, default: 1.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. Unlike ABAQUS, all time lengths defined are absolute time. There is no so-called "step time", which is related to some normalized time concept in ABAQUS.
  2. The Static step supports all matrix storage schemes.
  3. Displacement control solver MPDC is automatically enabled if a displacement load is active.
